title: Joseph in Egypt IQ
subtitle: From the pit to the palace, how well do you know Joseph's story?
about: From a coat of many colors to a pit, a prison, and finally a palace, Joseph's story is one of the Bible's longest and most detailed arcs, and one of its clearest pictures of God turning betrayal into rescue.

verses.text: And as for you, ye meant evil against me; but God meant it for good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.

questions.text: Who bought Joseph when he was first brought down to Egypt?

options.text: Pharaoh himself
options.explanation: Joseph did not meet Pharaoh until years later, when he interpreted the king's dreams.

options.text: Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh
options.explanation: Genesis 39:1 says Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard, bought Joseph from the Ishmaelites.

options.text: The chief baker
options.explanation: The chief baker was a fellow prisoner Joseph met later in jail, not the man who bought him.

options.text: A merchant in Goshen
options.explanation: Goshen became the home of Joseph's family much later. It was not where he was first sold.

questions.text: Why was Joseph thrown into prison in Egypt?

options.text: He was falsely accused by Potiphar's wife
options.explanation: Genesis 39 tells how Potiphar's wife lied about Joseph after he refused her, and he was put in prison.

options.text: He stole grain from Pharaoh's storehouse
options.explanation: Joseph was the one who later filled the storehouses. He was no thief.

options.text: He failed to interpret a dream
options.explanation: Joseph interpreted every dream put before him correctly. That was never the charge against him.

options.text: He led a revolt against Pharaoh
options.explanation: Joseph served faithfully wherever he was placed. There was no revolt.

questions.text: While in prison, whose two dreams did Joseph interpret?

options.text: Two of Pharaoh's sons
options.explanation: The dreamers were Pharaoh's servants, not his sons.

options.text: The chief butler and the chief baker
options.explanation: Genesis 40 describes Pharaoh's chief butler and chief baker, both jailed, each having a dream that Joseph explained.

options.text: Two Egyptian priests
options.explanation: No priests appear in this part of the story. The two dreamers were Pharaoh's officers.

options.text: Potiphar and his wife
options.explanation: Potiphar and his wife were back at the house. The prison dreams belonged to the butler and the baker.

questions.text: What did Pharaoh dream about that troubled him so deeply?

options.text: A great statue made of gold and clay
options.explanation: That dream belonged to King Nebuchadnezzar in the book of Daniel, not Pharaoh.

options.text: Seven cows and seven ears of grain
options.explanation: Genesis 41 tells of seven fat cows eaten by seven thin ones, and seven full ears swallowed by seven withered ears.

options.text: A ladder reaching up to heaven
options.explanation: The ladder was Jacob's dream at Bethel, generations earlier.

options.text: Stars bowing down to the moon
options.explanation: Joseph himself dreamed of the sun, moon, and stars bowing. Pharaoh's dream was about cows and grain.

questions.text: What did Joseph say the seven good years and seven bad years would be?

options.text: Seven years of war, then seven of peace
options.explanation: The dream was about food supply, not war and peace.

options.text: Seven years of plenty, then seven years of famine
options.explanation: Genesis 41 records that seven years of great plenty would come, followed by seven years of famine across the land.

options.text: Seven years of rain, then seven of flood
options.explanation: There was no flood here. The hardship was famine after a season of plenty.

options.text: Seven years of sickness, then seven of healing
options.explanation: Sickness was not part of the dream. It pointed to plenty and then famine.

questions.text: What position did Pharaoh give Joseph after he interpreted the dreams?

options.text: Chief priest of Egypt
options.explanation: Joseph was not made a priest. He was given charge over the whole land.

options.text: Ruler over all the land of Egypt, second only to Pharaoh
options.explanation: Genesis 41 says Pharaoh set Joseph over his house and all the land, keeping only the throne above him.

options.text: Captain of Pharaoh's army
options.explanation: Joseph's role was governing and storing food, not commanding soldiers.

options.text: Keeper of the royal vineyard
options.explanation: That was closer to the butler's old job. Joseph was put in charge of the entire nation.

questions.text: Why did Joseph's brothers travel to Egypt?

options.text: To find Joseph and apologize
options.explanation: They had no idea Joseph was alive, let alone ruling Egypt. They came for food.

options.text: To buy grain because of the famine
options.explanation: Genesis 42 says the famine reached Canaan, so Jacob sent his sons to Egypt to buy grain.

options.text: To trade with Pharaoh for gold
options.explanation: They came hungry, looking for food, not to trade for riches.

options.text: To escape a war in Canaan
options.explanation: There was no war. The trouble driving them was the famine.

questions.text: When Joseph finally revealed himself, how did he explain what his brothers had done?

options.text: He said God meant it for good, to save many lives
options.explanation: Genesis 50:20 (ASV) reads, "And as for you, ye meant evil against me; but God meant it for good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive."

options.text: He demanded they repay him in silver
options.explanation: Joseph asked for no payment. He pointed instead to God's purpose in it all.

options.text: He had them arrested for the crime
options.explanation: Joseph wept and forgave his brothers rather than punishing them.

options.text: He said he had forgotten the whole thing
options.explanation: Joseph remembered clearly, yet he chose to see God's hand at work for good.

questions.text: Where did Joseph settle his father and brothers when they came to Egypt?

options.text: In the land of Goshen
options.explanation: Genesis 47 records that Joseph gave his family the land of Goshen, a good area for their flocks.

options.text: Inside Pharaoh's palace
options.explanation: The family were shepherds, so they were given grazing land in Goshen rather than the palace.

options.text: On Mount Sinai
options.explanation: Mount Sinai belongs to the Exodus story under Moses, long after Joseph.

options.text: In the city of Babel
options.explanation: Babel was far away and far earlier in Genesis. Jacob's family settled in Goshen.

questions.text: How old was Joseph when he died, according to Genesis?

options.text: 70 years old
options.explanation: Joseph lived longer than that. The text gives a specific number at the close of Genesis.

options.text: 110 years old
options.explanation: Genesis 50:26 says Joseph died being a hundred and ten years old, and was put in a coffin in Egypt.

options.text: 120 years old
options.explanation: Moses lived to 120. Joseph's age at death was a hundred and ten.

options.text: 175 years old
options.explanation: That was Abraham's age at death. Joseph died at a hundred and ten.

questions.text: What did Joseph ask his family to do with his bones?

options.text: Bury them beside Pharaoh's tomb
options.explanation: Joseph did not want to stay in Egypt forever. He looked ahead to the land God promised.

options.text: Carry them up out of Egypt when God brought the people out
options.explanation: Genesis 50:25 says Joseph made the children of Israel swear to carry his bones up from Egypt one day.

options.text: Scatter them over the Nile
options.explanation: There is no such request in the text. Joseph wanted his bones carried to the promised land.

options.text: Keep them hidden in Goshen
options.explanation: Joseph was not asking to be hidden. He asked to be brought out when the people left Egypt.

questions.text: Looking back over the whole account, what is the big theme of Joseph's life in Egypt?

options.text: Revenge against those who hurt him
options.explanation: Joseph had every chance for revenge and chose forgiveness instead.

options.text: God's faithfulness and providence through hard seasons
options.explanation: From the pit to prison to the palace, the story shows God staying with Joseph and working through every setback.

options.text: The importance of building tall towers
options.explanation: That belongs to the tower of Babel, a different chapter entirely.

options.text: How to win battles in war
options.explanation: Joseph's story is not about warfare. It is about trust, forgiveness, and God's quiet care.

scoring.perfectMessage: From the pit to the palace, you know it all!

gradeBands.label: Just Starting
gradeBands.message: Joseph's story is waiting for you. Give it a read.

gradeBands.label: Getting There
gradeBands.message: You know the broad strokes. A reread will fill in the rest.

gradeBands.label: Well Studied
gradeBands.message: You clearly know Joseph's journey well.

gradeBands.label: Egypt Expert
gradeBands.message: Outstanding. Few know Joseph's story like you do.
